intro: Today pairs a solid technical core on agentic AI—what actually counts as an agent, why benchmarks and multi-agent demos mislead, and how to build and break the agent loop yourself—with a genuinely news-heavy banking day: US and EU regulators moving on AI-specific model risk, and three live deployment data points (JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, COBOL modernization) with a sharp rebuttal in the mix.

cards.title: Building Effective Agents
cards.bite: Most production AI systems that work well are simple, composable workflows—prompt chaining, routing, parallel calls—not fully autonomous agents that direct their own tool use. Reserve genuine agentic autonomy for cases where task complexity truly requires an LLM to decide its own steps, and only if you can accept the added latency and cost. This is the primary source nearly all other 'agent architecture' content on the web is paraphrasing.
cards.read_if: Read if you want the foundational vocabulary to tell a real agent from a scripted pipeline; skip if you've already read it.
cards.key_takeaway: Most production systems that work well are simple, composable workflows (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization) rather than fully autonomous agents; add agentic autonomy only when task complexity genuinely requires an LLM to direct its own tool use and you can tolerate the latency/cost tradeoff.

cards.title: AI Agents That Matter
cards.source: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir, Narayanan (Princeton) — arXiv
cards.bite: Agent benchmark leaderboards that report accuracy without controlling for cost are misleading, because expensive retry-heavy architectures can look artificially strong against simple, cheap baselines. A rigorous evaluation has to report both accuracy and cost together, or the ranking is close to meaningless. This gives a citable, academic basis for challenging 'which agent scores highest' as the wrong question.
cards.read_if: Read if you need a rigorous, citable rebuttal to leaderboard claims; skip if the one-line takeaway is enough for you.
cards.key_takeaway: Agent benchmarks that report accuracy without controlling for cost are misleading — simple baseline strategies can match complex, expensive agent architectures at a fraction of the cost, so any honest evaluation must report both.

cards.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
cards.bite: Analyzing over 1,600 traces from seven popular multi-agent frameworks, researchers found most failures aren't model limitations but design failures—poor task specification, agents losing track of role or conversation history, and weak verification of outputs. That means better orchestration design fixes more problems than swapping in a bigger model. The paper offers a concrete taxonomy for diagnosing exactly why a multi-agent demo breaks.
cards.read_if: Read if you regularly troubleshoot or need to explain a failing multi-agent demo; skip if you don't work with multi-agent setups.
cards.key_takeaway: Across 1,600+ traces from 7 popular multi-agent frameworks, most failures are not model limitations but organizational/design failures — bad task specification, agents losing track of conversation history or role, and weak verification of outputs — meaning better orchestration design fixes more than a bigger model would.

cards.title: Building an AI agent from scratch in Python
cards.bite: This walks through building the core agent loop—an LLM, a tool-calling step, and a while-loop that runs until the task completes—using direct API calls, no framework. The point is to see exactly what LangChain, CrewAI, and similar frameworks are abstracting away before you adopt one or evaluate a vendor's use of one.
cards.read_if: Read if you want hands-on grounding in tool-calling mechanics; skip if you're not going to write code.
cards.key_takeaway: Before adopting LangChain/CrewAI/etc., implement the agent loop yourself with direct API calls — an Agent class, a tool-calling step, and a while-loop until task completion — so you understand what the framework is actually abstracting away.

cards.title: Ten AI Agents Destroyed Production. Zero Postmortems.
cards.bite: A compilation of ten real, documented incidents—including a coding agent that ran a destructive infrastructure command against live production—makes the case that non-bypassable confirmation gates for destructive actions and full command-level audit logging are production-readiness requirements, not nice-to-haves. These are concrete, real-world examples rather than hypothetical risk scenarios.
cards.read_if: Read if you need real incident stories to counter 'just let the agent handle it'; skip if you already have your own.
cards.key_takeaway: Destructive actions (database drops, terraform destroy, rm -rf) need non-bypassable confirmation gates as a hard default, and full command-level audit logging should be treated as a production-readiness requirement, not a nice-to-have.

cards.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns: A Practical Guide
cards.bite: Comparing orchestrator-worker, hierarchical, fan-out, swarm, and mesh patterns on latency, fault tolerance, and debuggability, the guide argues orchestrator-worker should be the default for production because it gives clear accountability and predictable cost. Escalate to hierarchical or fan-out only when worker count or genuine task parallelism demands it—swarm and mesh remain niche and hard to debug.
cards.read_if: Read if you need a decision rule for when multi-agent complexity is actually worth it; skip if you only work with single-agent systems.
cards.key_takeaway: Default to the orchestrator-worker pattern for production systems because it gives clear accountability and predictable cost; only escalate to hierarchical or fan-out patterns when worker count or task parallelism specifically demands it — swarm/mesh patterns remain niche and hard to debug.

cards.title: Model Risk Management: Revised Guidance (OCC Bulletin 2026-13)
cards.source: OCC (with Federal Reserve Board and FDIC)
cards.bite: US banking regulators rescinded the 2011 model-risk guidance and the 2021 BSA/AML model-risk statement, replacing them with non-enforceable, risk-based guidance—and explicitly flagged that a forthcoming request for information will address generative and agentic AI model risk specifically, meaning current guidance doesn't yet cover it. The framework banks cite as governing is mid-transition, which reshapes what governance tooling they'll need next.
cards.read_if: Read if you sell into US banks; skip if your accounts are entirely outside US-regulated banking.
cards.key_takeaway: The agencies made MRM guidance non-enforceable and risk-based rather than prescriptive, and have explicitly flagged that a forthcoming request for information will address generative and agentic AI model risk specifically — the current guidance does not yet cover it.

cards.title: BaFin Guidance on ICT Risks in the Use of AI at Financial Entities
cards.bite: Germany's financial regulator ruled that generative AI and large language models get no special exemption under EU digital-resilience rules—they're ICT assets subject to the same third-party, resilience-testing, and outsourcing requirements as any core banking system. The guidance includes a case study of a bank running an LLM assistant across different infrastructures, showing exactly how existing risk-treatment rules apply to a live deployment.
cards.read_if: Read if you sell into EU banks; skip if your accounts are entirely US-based.
cards.key_takeaway: AI systems—particularly generative AI and large language models—must be fully embedded into existing ICT governance, testing, and third-party risk frameworks, with heightened supervisory scrutiny, and BaFin's guidance includes a case study of an institution running an LLM assistant across different infrastructures to illustrate how CRR and Solvency II risk treatment applies.

cards.title: JPMorgan Chase plans to deploy more powerful AI agents this year
cards.bite: JPMorgan's chief analytics officer says AI is already boosting business results—a 20% increase in private banking gross sales, and a potential 50% expansion in banker client coverage—but fully autonomous, long-running agents still aren't cleared for corporate use because of security concerns. It's a credible peer benchmark on what's actually shipping at the largest US bank versus what remains blocked.
cards.read_if: Read if you need a grounded reference point for realistic bank AI timelines; skip if you already track JPMorgan's statements closely.
cards.key_takeaway: JPMorgan says AI is already boosting business results, including a 20% increase in private banking gross sales, and could eventually allow bankers to expand client coverage by as much as 50%, but fully autonomous long-running agents aren't yet cleared for corporate use because of security concerns.

cards.title: How AI helps break the cost barrier to COBOL modernization
cards.bite: Anthropic claims its agentic coding tool can automate the exploration and analysis phases of COBOL modernization—mapping dependencies, documenting workflows, identifying risks—the phases that consume most of the effort, letting teams modernize legacy codebases in quarters instead of years. This single post moved IBM's stock 13% in a day and is now the standard reference point in legacy-modernization conversations, but it addresses only the discovery bottleneck, not full migration.
cards.read_if: Read if a prospect has raised this post or COBOL modernization with you; skip otherwise.
cards.key_takeaway: Claude Code, Anthropic's agentic coding tool, can automate the exploration and analysis phases that consume most of the effort in COBOL modernization — mapping dependencies, documenting workflows, identifying risks — which is what lets teams modernize a COBOL codebase in quarters instead of years, but this addresses the discovery bottleneck, not the full migration.

cards.title: Claude Code and COBOL modernization: What's the reality?
cards.bite: Thoughtworks, drawing on 18 months of hands-on legacy modernization work, pushes back directly on the assumption that Anthropic's coding-assistant gains mean COBOL modernization is now solved—the hard parts, like business scoping, behavioral equivalence, and organizational change, remain largely untouched by these tools. This is the counter-narrative to have ready when a prospect assumes the problem is fully automated.
cards.read_if: Read if you've discussed or will discuss the Anthropic COBOL post with an account; skip if that topic never comes up.
cards.key_takeaway: Thoughtworks says it would be wrong for onlookers to assume the market reaction means COBOL knowledge is now obsolete and modernization has been fully automated — the hard parts (business scoping, behavioral equivalence, organizational change) are largely untouched by the coding-assistant gains Anthropic highlighted.

cards.title: Wells Fargo Scales AI to Meet Surging Customer Demand
cards.bite: Wells Fargo's AI virtual assistant passed 1 billion customer interactions in under three years, while mobile active users grew from 31.8 million to 33.5 million year-over-year—a second named, quantified example beyond JPMorgan showing that customer-facing conversational AI can scale inside a heavily regulated retail bank.
cards.read_if: Read if you need a second peer reference point beyond JPMorgan; skip if you already cite Wells Fargo's numbers.
cards.key_takeaway: Wells Fargo reported that Fargo, its AI-powered virtual assistant, reached over 1 billion customer interactions less than three years since launch, while mobile active users grew from 31.8 million to 33.5 million year-over-year — evidence that customer-facing conversational AI can scale in a heavily regulated retail bank.
